thread.title: Tech Stocks: Great Earnings Season Or Export Controls?

author: Elazar Advisors, LLC
title: Tech Stocks: Great Earnings Season Or Export Controls?
text:
Intel ( INTC ) had a big news day last Thursday. For investors though there was one key stat that helped confirm a tech boom. Intel's revenue growth accelerated once again which confirms something we've been seeing from many tech giants. What better stat is there than accelerating revenue growth to get bullish on tech?
But just a couple of days later to counter Intel's great numbers there's been a new fly buzzing bothering markets. While many are focused on legislation that would limit foreign investments my biggest concern is the chance for export controls. The best in tech who have exposure to China now have a realistic risk to their revenues, as we'll explain.
Taking the two together makes tech tough. We'll tell you our approach.
First, Confirmation of What Appeared To Be An Amazing Earnings Season To Come Intel was the first tech company that previewed Q2 on Thursday. Here's what they said .
"Intel expects to deliver a record second quarter, with revenues of approximately $16.9 billion and non-GAAP EPS of approximately $0.99. With accelerating data-centric revenue, the company is off to an excellent start in the first half of the year and expects 2018 to be another record year."
Let's see what that revenue number means in context.
2017 2017 2018 2018 Q3 Q4 Q1 Q2 A E Revenue 16149 17053 16066 16900 YOY 2.4% 4.1% 8.6% 14.5% 2yr 11.4% 13.9% 16.6% 23.6% QTQ 9.4% 5.6% -5.8% 5.2% Look at the one-year revenue growth go from 2.4% to 14.5% in a mere four quarters.
Now you all know I love the 2-year. That's the true-tell. Look at that two-year revenue growth go from 11.4% to 23.6% in a mere four quarters.
Which way is this business going? Revenues are accelerating.
We use the two-year to make sure a company's not just benefiting from easier year-ago comparisons or one time dips. The two-year adds this year's quarter's growth to last year's same quarter's growth.
Intel's accelerating two-year growth tells you something strong is underlying in their performance.
And It's Not Just Intel Intel being the first reporter of the second quarter earnings season gives a sneak peak into the others in tech.
And remember that Intel's revenue acceleration is in the face of AMD killing them, Spectre, Meltdown, CEO issues, node transition issues, kitchen sink issues, all types of issues; and business is still very very strong.
So if Intel's business reports stronger and stronger with all that and the kitchen sink, how do you think AMD or NVIDIA are doing with their better trajectories? Probably at least as good, maybe even better.
Intel's a pretty big important company, right? If they are doing well it's a good sign for overall tech, right?
But what we love is for the last few quarters Intel wasn't alone. Many huge players in tech were seeing the same thing, revenues accelerate.
Let's look.
And remember, our key stat is super-simple revenue growth. Is revenue growth growing faster or slower. And for an added check let's look at the two year.
Before we heard about "export controls" we were revving up to get bullish on earnings.
Here's many large companies all showing the same revenue acceleration.

That's a pretty powerful list, yes? We have all the FANG stocks in there along with Intel, Microsoft and Cisco who were tech darlings of the past.
Tech Fundamentals Getting Better Why are so many companies seeing this acceleration in their key business metric.
For one the economy's picking up. The Atlanta Fed is expecting faster GDP in Q2 than we had in Q1.
Tax breaks are freeing up tech spending.
As we speak to our tech company contacts we are also hearing that traditional companies, known as enterprise, are also starting to spend for the first time in a decade. Traditional companies, not just the big cloud titans are starting to add to the tech spending pool.
So far the big cloud/hyperscalers like Miscrosoft, Google, Facebook and Amazon were enough to drive this tech boom as they raced for market share.
But now spending is spreading out to the rest of the world, not just the top seven-or-so tech spenders. And there are many more traditional companies with a bigger collective budget than the few hyperscalers.
That's one key reason for this acceleration across the board at major tech players. The number of companies finally spending is broadening out.
Enterprise Has Been Getting Better And Is Much Bigger Than Hyperscaler Spending Look at what Intel said on their Q1 call ,
"And we also saw growth in our enterprise segments for the second consecutive quarter, as macro strength continued and customers prioritized hybrid and on-premises infrastructure investments."
How many quarters are we into this new leg of tech spend? Two quarters? Come on, that is just too ridiculous. If we are only two quarters in, how many more quarters does this have the potential to go?
Tech spending lasted all of the '90s.
Since the 2008 top, tech spending's been much slower.
It's just starting to pick up.
While traditional companies have been expanding their exposure to cloud providers like Amazon's AWS and Microsoft's Azure, they are starting to build out their own tech infrastructure once again.
That's why Microsoft, Intel and Cisco are finally starting to see a pickup.
Traditional companies are going through an upgrade cycle of their own right now.
That's why Intel's last quarter saw their PC business up for the first time in a few quarters. That's a key reason why Microsoft saw a big jump in their PC related business last quarter.
Cloud companies are the spending leaders but the rest of the world has a larger collective wallet to spend. It looks like spending was just about to start spreading out.
Now For The Fly In The Ointment: Export Control (cue change for background music)
So amazing earnings right?
Just when I had my eye on a huge breakout for tech earnings in Q2 and beyond we have something staring us down that is not so pretty and not so easy to ignore.
While the market seems to be focused on foreign investment caps in tech we're more concerned with the export control story that the US is pushing forward.
Export controls mean that the US could stop US companies from selling to China if they think the US company's IP was at risk to getting stolen.
It was reported in the NY Times this week as follows ,
"The officials also said Mr. Trump will direct the heads of the Commerce Department and other federal agencies to review the nation’s existing system of export controls and recommend any needed changes. That could have a more significant effect on United States companies than restrictions on Chinese investment, since it would limit the ability of American companies to sell a range of products to China. The White House has targeted specific products that it wants to prevent China from dominating, including robotics, artificial intelligence and new energy vehicles."
It's been recently reported that Micron ( MU ) has been broken into several times with the goal to take intellectual property ("IP") to China.
Somebody at Micron apparently told Axios that China's recent office "visits" or raids in the guise of antitrust probes were a cover to take IP secrets.
"They want access to the intellectual property. They need us to teach them how to do it. Once they have the industry, they want to push us out."
Many business relationships in China apparently force handing over IP to enter the market.
China has said they plan not to steal IP but obviously that's what's bothering Trump and the push for export control.
How Would Export Control Affect Tech? If export controls were put into effect it would potentially stop some revenues to China. I have to consider that in my earnings models.
What's the company going to earn in the next 12 months? I'm not so sure. Will the US stop a portion of their revenues exposed to China? If so my numbers would be too high. This needs to get clarified and this very topic, export controls, I think has been the underlying driver in the market's weakness this week.
Let's look at some round numbers and see what large tech companies are exposed to China export control risk.
AMD had 33% of their 2017 revenues to China and Taiwan according to their 10K
Apple had about 20% of their 2017 sales from China.
Applied Materials ( AMAT ) had 19% of their 2017 revenues from China.
Applied Optoelectronics ( AAOI ) had 32% of their 2017 sales from China according to their 10K .
Intel had 23% of their 2017 revenues to China.
Micron had about 50% of their 2017 sales from China.
NVIDIA had 20% of their 2017 sales from China according to their 10k .
Qualcomm ( QCOM ) had 65% of their 2017 revenues from China (including Hong Kong) and South Korea.
Tesla had 23% of their 2017 deliveries to China according to their 10K .
Texas Instruments had 44% of their 2017 revenues from China.
These are all major players in tech. Would their IP be considered deer enough to the US not to let it get into China's hands?
The heating up of this topic seemed to accelerate over the last few weeks. Ever since reports came out about Micron's Chinese office "visits" US' focus on this topic appears to have picked up.
The "export controls" would limit sales to China for key technologies the US calls "industrial significant."
Is the IP of the above companies "industrial significant?" Probably so, right?
We'd guess that some portion of that revenue exposure to China comes into question if "export control" legislation advances.
That's what we're watching.
We've spoken to some companies and we think this could turn into a mess if enacted. Asia's supply chain would become confused if some components were not allowed in. How do you complete production without necessary component parts.
Most important though would be the impact to our earnings models. Earnings drive stocks. If revenues disappear because of "export control" then earnings estimates and price targets would have to come down. That's a risk to the stock prices.
The US decision to penalize ZTE crashed ZTE's revenues and ZTE almost went out of business. Export controls could impact US companies to a smaller degree but in the same direction.
We hope there's a trade resolution soon.
How Are We Dealing With This Dichotomy
On the one hand Intel hints to an accelerated earnings season. On the other hand do I need to factor in export controls to my earnings numbers? Not sure.
Here's the way we're dealing with it.
I think in this period smaller portfolio exposure makes the most sense. We're telling subscribers that it probably makes sense to build closer to earnings events if we don't have clarity about export controls. This, in effect reduces market exposure.
If we get confirmation that export control is a near term risk and that its quickly planned to be used after passing legislation we need to watch out. It may not matter how much you love a company, their earnings would have risk.
If we get a settlement between the US and China then build back to normal position sizes.
That's how we're thinking about it.
Conclusion
So while tech has the potential for amazing results in Q2 we're facing a very real issue with potential "export controls" legislation.
We're hoping for a trade resolution soon.
